observable_outcome: The in-memory adapter settles its reservation the way the real one does, so a test that reads a handful of times no longer exhausts a day's budget and a passing test means the same thing on both adapters. Measured at 9a09ef8: internal/application/service.go:131 reserves quota.ReadTransactionUsage (6,001 reads) for every read transaction; internal/store/firestore settles it (trueUpQuota, store.go:474-497, actual = len(u.cache) reads and len(u.values) writes, fed by countReads at 13 call sites, applied in flush() before any write); internal/store/memory's whole quota implementation is one line, ReserveQuota at store.go:167-169, and nothing settles it. 25,000 / 6,001 means exactly four read transactions fit in a UTC day on the in-memory adapter, which is why V2-079's seven-page walk advances an injected clock 25 hours per page (memory/store_test.go:836) and why two other tests are split with comments calling the limit a production property. The repair instruments the in-memory adapter to count the distinct record keys it actually read and wrote -- mirroring Firestore's document set, probe row and missing-document read included -- and to call quota.Counter.TrueUp on the cloned working state before the swap. Completeness is enforced by a guard derived from the port interface, agreement is asserted by one test name in both adapter packages over one shared workload table, and the injected-clock workaround is removed. No budget is raised, nothing is reserved after the work, and internal/quota is byte-unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: A1. Scope boundary, written into all four evidence records BEFORE any code is edited, as a table with one row each. (1) What this task makes true: the in-memory adapter settles its worst-case reservation to the reads and writes it actually made, so a read transaction costs what it cost on the Firestore adapter and many read transactions fit in one simulated day. (2) What it deliberately does not do: it raises no budget (internal/quota is prohibited and byte-unchanged), it moves no reservation to after the work (internal/application/service.go is prohibited), it reimplements no correction (quota.Counter.TrueUp is reused), it changes no adapter's stored data, it changes no route and no response, and it changes nothing in internal/store/firestore/store.go -- that adapter is the specification here. (3) What it records but does not fix: any workload row where the two adapters' measured usage disagrees (A6 requires it be reported, never forced), and the fact that neither adapter has a delete operation so the deletes component is always zero. (4) What only a later task can establish: nothing. (5) That this task passes no release gate on its own, and that it is the last source change before V2-080's live re-observation.

A2. Baseline, measured before changing anything. Top-level test counts read by grep at 9a09ef8: internal/store/memory 13, internal/store/firestore 35, internal/api 54, internal/application 180, internal/quota 14, internal/contracts 33. Also re-measure: the number of methods on the in-memory adapter's unit (70 at 9a09ef8), the number of countReads call sites in internal/store/firestore/store.go (13), and the four-read-transactions-per-day figure (quota.DefaultBudget.Reads / quota.ReadTransactionUsage.Reads). Record before and after test counts per touched package; the after count must be the before count plus exactly the tests A5, A6, A7 and A8 add, and no existing test may be deleted or renamed.

A3. Reproduce the defect yourself before fixing it, and record the argv and the verdict of each reproduction. (a) On the in-memory adapter, drive five consecutive read transactions on ONE fixed injected instant and record that the fifth is refused with quota.ErrOverBudget while the first four succeed. (b) Run the identical five against the Firestore adapter under the emulator and record that all five succeed and that the committed daily total is a small multiple of a single page's real cost. (c) Record the exact source asymmetry with line numbers: internal/store/firestore/store.go's trueUpQuota and countReads against internal/store/memory/store.go's one-line ReserveQuota. (d) Record that the same store-firestore command WITHOUT the emulator is green because the cases skip, and state in those words that such a run measures nothing and is never a pass (gate rule G7).

A4. The counting rule, implemented exactly as dp-v2-087 d2 states it and documented in the adapter's own comments with the Firestore line it mirrors: a key counts once per transaction; a MISS counts as one read; a paged read counts min(limit+1, rows remaining after the cursor) because the Firestore query is Limit(limit+1); the quota record counts as one read and one write; a write counts its key once; a single-key read of a key already written in the same transaction counts nothing; deletes stay zero. Keys are namespaced by kind so two aggregates sharing an id are two documents. The true-up runs inside Store.Transact after the callback returns nil and BEFORE the working clone is swapped in, so a failed transaction drops the reservation and the correction together. Reuse quota.Counter.TrueUp; do not write a second correction and do not touch internal/quota.

A5. Completeness, enforced mechanically. Extend internal/store/memory/source_guard_test.go -- which already parses the package with go/ast -- with TestEveryUnitOfWorkMethodCountsWhatItReadOrWrote: enumerate the method set of application.UnitOfWork by reflection over the interface type, and fail if the corresponding method on the adapter's unit contains no call to a counting helper. Any exemption is an explicit allow-list entry with a one-line justification for why that method touches no record. Report the measured method count and the allow-list in the evidence. If the guard cannot be written against the port interface, stop and escalate rather than shipping the instrumentation without it: a hand-written method list is not an acceptable substitute, because it is exactly what goes stale.

A6. THE CROSS-ADAPTER ASSERTION, one name in BOTH packages: TestBothAdaptersSettleTheSameReservationForTheSameWorkload, in internal/store/memory/store_test.go and internal/store/firestore/quota_integration_test.go. Same workload rows in both files -- a bounded first page at page_size 1, the same page at page_size 2, a Requirement detail read, and a capture mutation -- each asserting the committed daily Usage after the transaction against the SAME literal expectation written in both files, with a comment in each saying the two literals must stay identical and why. Record both measurements side by side in the evidence. If a row disagrees, STOP AND ESCALATE: do not adjust either literal, do not delete the row, and do not widen the expectation into a range or a tolerance. The Firestore half runs under scripts/firestore-emulator.sh; without the emulator it skips and measures nothing.

A7. The outcome, asserted directly: TestManyReadTransactionsFitInOneDayOnTheInMemoryAdapter. On ONE fixed injected instant, run a number of consecutive read transactions derived from quota.DefaultBudget.Reads divided by the measured trued-up cost of one read transaction -- not a round number chosen for comfort -- assert every one succeeds, and assert the committed daily total afterwards is far below quota.DefaultBudget.Reads. Assert the same for writes over a run of mutations. A test that only checks 'no error' is not sufficient: the committed total is what distinguishes a settled reservation from a raised budget (non_goals item 1) and from no reservation at all (non_goals item 2).
